accroche: After the eruption of Tambora in April 1815, the summer of 1816 is one of the coldest in Western Europe. In Geneva, it also rains 80% more.
contenu_vulgarise:
What we remember of the summer of 1816 is the cold: “the year without a summer.” The records digitized since then say something more precise, and stranger.

## A volcano, a veil of sulfur

From April 5 to 10, 1815, Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa, in present-day Indonesia, erupted. It was an eruption of Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) 7. The plume sent sulfur gases into the stratosphere, where they turned into sulfate aerosols. For about three years, these aerosols intercepted part of the solar radiation.

The average drop remained modest: 0.4 to 0.8 °C per year, compared with the previous thirty years, for the tropics and the extratropical Northern Hemisphere.

## A cold, cloudy, rainy summer

The summer of 1816 was nonetheless one of the coldest measured over much of Western Europe, from central Scandinavia to the Mediterranean, with the maximum anomaly over Switzerland and eastern France. Farther east, the few series from Russia and Ukraine indicate on the contrary a milder summer. In the Central England temperature series, which goes back to 1659, it is the third coldest summer, after 1725 and 1695.

In Geneva, records taken twice a day have been digitized. The afternoon is hit harder than the morning: the departure reaches −3.8 °C, against −1.8 °C at dawn, relative to the 1799-1821 period with the disturbed years removed. Summer precipitation increases by 80%, low-pressure situations triple, and high-pressure situations disappear.

The authors explain this by increased cloud cover, which is well documented: it accounts both for the stronger afternoon cooling and for the disappearance of mornings milder than average.

## A shift in weather types

We picture a volcano turning down a thermostat. The records show something else: a shift in weather types, with more lows, more clouds, and a stronger westerly and northwesterly flow toward Europe. Very low temperatures at dawn were no more frequent than before; what was missing were the mornings milder than average.

And Tambora is not the only factor. The 1810s are the coldest decade in comparable European series, which begin in the 1780s. An eruption in 1808 or 1809, whose origin is still unknown, shows up clearly in ice cores. According to the authors, a large share of the weather-type anomalies of 1816 also probably stems from natural variability.

The most famous summer in climatology therefore has several causes, some of which we can now tell apart.

repere.texte: In the twice-daily Geneva records, the summer of 1816 shows 80% more precipitation, three times as many low-pressure situations, and no high-pressure situations at all.
repere.source: Raible et al., “Tambora 1815 as a test case for high impact volcanic eruptions: Earth system effects,” WIREs Climate Change, 2016

carte.punch: 1816 was not only cold: in Geneva, it rained 80% more.
carte.idee: Tambora (April 1815) did not just lower a thermometer. In Geneva, the summer of 1816 has 80% more rain and three times as many low-pressure situations: weather types flipped, and afternoons are hit harder than mornings.

quiz.question: Why, in Geneva, are the afternoons of summer 1816 hit harder than the dawns?
choix: Because Tambora's aerosols block only afternoon radiation
Because the thermometers of the time would go out of calibration in the heat
Because the north wind blew mostly after noon
Because increased cloud cover cut off the afternoon heating
quiz.explication: The departure reaches −3.8 °C in the afternoon against −1.8 °C at dawn. The authors attribute it to clouds and the change in weather types. Aerosols do not filter only in the afternoon, and nothing suggests a flaw in the digitized thermometer records.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Central England temperature series say about the summer of 1816?
choix: It is the coldest summer since 1659
It is the third coldest summer since 1659
It is warmer than those of 1695 and 1725
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Raible et al., 1816 is the third coldest summer in the series since 1659, after 1725 and 1695.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the Russian and Ukrainian series indicate for the summer of 1816?
choix: Nothing, for lack of sufficient records in the east
A summer milder than Western Europe's
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that the few series from Russia and Ukraine indicate on the contrary a milder summer, the opposite of the cold observed in Western Europe.
